title: The system: an online store's product cache with a client-side ring
caption: Every app server holds the same ring in memory and picks the cache node itself; a membership service only changes the ring when nodes come and go.

steps.text: A shopper opens a product page. The load balancer sends the request to any app server: they are stateless and interchangeable.
Each app server keeps the ring in memory: a sorted array of vnode tokens, pushed by the membership service whenever it changes. No lookup service sits on the request path.
hash("product:42") lands between two tokens; a binary search finds the next token clockwise, which belongs to Cache B. One hop, decided locally.
Hit: Cache B answers in under a millisecond. The other caches never see this key.
Miss: read the product from the catalog DB and write it back to the same node with a TTL, so the next request for that key hits.
Emit hit rate and per-node key share. A node holding far more than its share, or a sudden hit-rate drop, means the ring or a key is misbehaving.

scenarios.name: Scale out for a sale
scenarios.summary: Adding a node moves only the keys on its new arcs; the database sees a short bump, not a stampede.

steps.text: A flash sale starts and the caches run hot. The autoscaler boots Cache D and registers it with the membership service.
Membership places D's 128 tokens on the ring and pushes the new version; every app server swaps its array atomically.
Keys that now fall just before one of D's tokens move to D, about a quarter of them. They miss once there.
Those misses fill from the catalog DB. A, B and C keep roughly three quarters of their keys hot.

scenarios.name: Cache B crashes
scenarios.summary: B's arcs fall to the next tokens clockwise, which belong to many nodes, so its load spreads out instead of doubling one neighbour.

steps.text: Cache B stops answering; calls for its keys time out after 20 ms.
After 3 failed health checks, membership removes B and pushes a ring without its tokens.
Each of B's 128 arcs now belongs to whichever token comes next, so the keys scatter across A and C.
About a third of the keys miss at once. Coalesce concurrent misses so the DB reads each key once, not once per request.
Hit rate dips and recovers within a few minutes as A and C warm.

scenarios.name: Ring rollout lags
scenarios.summary: While app servers disagree about the ring, some keys have two owners: a write goes to one, a read comes from the other.

steps.text: An operator replaces Cache C with a box twice the size and doubles its weight to 256 tokens.
The push reaches half the app servers; the rest still run the old ring for a few seconds.
A price update invalidates the key on its new owner C; a server on the old ring still reads the stale price from B.
Mitigate: carry the ring version in metrics and alert on mixed versions, invalidate on both old and new owners during a rollout, and keep TTLs short.
